title: The Olympic Games: Then and Now
summary: How the Olympic Games began in ancient Greece, how they were revived, what the rings mean, how the Paralympics began, and why training and fair play matter.
poll: Playing fairly is more important than winning.

versions.title: The Games
versions.text:
Every four years, the best athletes meet. They come from all over the world. They run, swim, jump, and throw. This is the Olympic Games. But the Games are very old.

The first Games were held in Greece. It was in ancient times. That was more than two thousand years ago. Men came from far and wide to compete. They ran races. They boxed. They raced carts. Horses pulled them. The prize was not gold. It was a crown made of olive leaves.

The old Games came to an end. Then, in 1896, they came back. A man from France helped bring them back. Now men and women from more than 200 lands take part.

The Games have a flag with five rings. The rings join. They are a symbol. They stand for all parts of the world. They come as friends.

There are Games for people with a disability, too. Some athletes race in a chair with wheels. Some cannot see. They are fast and strong.

It is hard to get to the Games. Athletes train for years. They work with coaches.

Most of all, they play fair. They do not cheat. They shake hands. A fair game is a good game.

versions.title: The Olympic Games
versions.text:
Every four years, the best athletes on Earth come together. They run, swim, jump, and throw. This big event is the Olympic Games. But did you know the Games began a long time ago?

The first Games took place in ancient Greece. That was more than two thousand years ago. They were held in a place called Olympia. Men came from many Greek towns to compete. They ran races. They wrestled and boxed. Some raced in carts pulled by horses. The winners did not get gold. Each one got a crown made of olive leaves.

The old Games came to an end. Then a man from France had an idea. His name was Pierre de Coubertin. He wanted to bring the Games back. In 1896, the new Games were held in Athens, Greece. Now men and women from more than 200 lands take part.

The Olympic flag has five rings that link. The rings are a symbol. They stand for all parts of the world as friends.

There are Games for athletes with a disability, too. They are called the Paralympic Games. Some athletes race in wheelchairs. Some cannot see, so a guide runs next to them.

It is hard to get to the Games. Athletes train for years. They eat good food and get rest. They work with their coaches.

Most of all, athletes must play fair. They keep the rules. They do not cheat. They shake hands, win or lose.

versions.title: The Olympic Games: Then and Now
versions.text:
Every four years, the best athletes in the world meet in one city. They run, swim, jump, and throw. Each one hopes to win a medal. This huge event is the Olympic Games. But the story of the Games began long, long ago.

The first Olympic Games took place in ancient Greece. That was more than 2,700 years ago. They were held at Olympia, a holy place for the Greeks. Men came from many Greek cities to compete. At first, there was just one event. It was a short race. Later, they added wrestling, boxing, and chariot races. Winners did not get gold medals. Each one got a crown made of olive leaves.

The old Games ended long ago. Then a Frenchman named Pierre de Coubertin made a plan to bring them back. In 1896, the first modern Games were held in Athens, Greece. Today, men and women from more than 200 nations take part.

The Olympic flag shows five rings that link. The rings are a symbol. They stand for the parts of the world coming together as friends.

The Paralympic Games are for athletes with a disability. Some race in wheelchairs. Some are blind and run with a guide. These Games are held in the same city, soon after the Olympics.

To reach the Games, athletes train for years. They practice most days. They eat healthy food, get lots of sleep, and work with coaches.

Fair play is at the heart of the Games. Athletes must follow the rules. They must respect the other team and never cheat.

versions.title: The Olympic Games: Then and Now
versions.text:
Every four years, thousands of the world's best athletes gather in one host city. They sprint, swim, leap, and throw, and each hopes to win a medal for their country. This huge event is the Olympic Games. Its story goes back nearly three thousand years.

The first Olympic Games took place in ancient Greece. Historians usually date the first recorded Games to 776 BCE. They were held at Olympia, a holy site where the Greeks honored Zeus, the chief of their gods. Men traveled from Greek cities near and far to compete. Only men could take part. At first, there was only one event, a sprint of about 190 meters. Over time, wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing were added. Champions did not win gold medals. Instead, each winner was crowned with a wreath of olive leaves. This was a great honor.

The ancient Games came to an end about 1,600 years ago. Centuries later, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin decided to revive them. He believed that sport could build healthy young people and help nations live in peace. In 1896, the first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, with athletes from 14 countries. Today, athletes from more than 200 nations take part, and women compete in nearly every sport.

The Olympic flag shows five rings that link together. Coubertin chose the rings to represent the parts of the world joining in friendship.

The Paralympic Games are for athletes with a disability. Some race in wheelchairs, and blind runners race beside a guide. Today, the Paralympics take place in the same city, shortly after the Olympics.

Reaching the Games takes years of training. Athletes practice almost daily. They eat healthy meals, sleep well, and work on their skills with coaches.

Above all, the Games celebrate fair play. Athletes promise to follow the rules, respect every opponent, and compete honestly.

versions.title: The Olympic Games: An Ancient Idea Reborn

Every four years, thousands of the world's finest athletes assemble in a single host city to sprint, swim, leap, and throw before a global audience. This enormous international event is the Olympic Games, and its history stretches back nearly three thousand years to a peaceful valley in southern Greece.

The earliest Olympic Games took place in ancient Greece, and historians generally date the first recorded competition to 776 BCE. The festival was held at Olympia, a sacred sanctuary dedicated to Zeus, and it was so respected that a truce allowed athletes and spectators to travel there safely, even when Greek cities were in conflict. Only men were permitted to compete. Initially, the program consisted of a single sprint of approximately 190 meters, but organizers gradually introduced wrestling, boxing, and chariot racing. Champions received no gold medals; instead, each winner was crowned with a wreath of olive leaves, an honor that brought fame to both the athlete and his city.

The ancient Games came to an end approximately 1,600 years ago. Centuries later, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin resolved to revive them, convinced that athletic competition could develop healthy young people and encourage peaceful relationships between nations. The Olympic flag displays five interlocking rings in blue, yellow, black, green, and red on a white background. Coubertin designed the rings to symbolize the continents of the world united in friendship, and he observed that every national flag contained at least one of these colors.

The Paralympic Games grew from a sports competition organized in England in 1948 by Dr. Ludwig Guttmann, a doctor who used sport in the rehabilitation of injured soldiers. The first Paralympic Games were held in Rome in 1960, and today they take place in the same host city shortly after the Olympics.

Qualifying for either event demands years of discipline. Athletes train almost daily, follow carefully planned diets, and analyze their technique with experienced coaches.

Above all, the Games celebrate fair play. Athletes pledge to obey the rules and respect every opponent, because integrity matters more than any single victory.

versions.title: The Olympic Games: An Ancient Idea Reborn
versions.text:
Every four years, thousands of the world's most accomplished athletes assemble within a single host city to sprint, swim, leap, and throw before an enormous global television audience. This international celebration is the Olympic Games, and its history stretches back nearly three thousand years to a tranquil valley situated in the western Peloponnese, a mountainous region of southern Greece.

The earliest Olympic Games took place in ancient Greece, and historians generally date the first formally recorded competition to 776 BCE. The festival itself was held at Olympia, a sacred sanctuary dedicated to Zeus. It was so universally respected throughout the ancient Greek world that a formal truce allowed athletes and spectators alike to travel there safely, even during periods when neighboring Greek city-states were actively engaged in military conflict with one another. Only men, however, were permitted to compete in these ancient contests. Initially, the entire program consisted of a single sprint measuring approximately 190 meters, but organizers progressively introduced wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and various other physically demanding contests over subsequent centuries. Champions received no gold medals whatsoever; instead, each victor was crowned with a simple wreath of olive leaves, a modest-seeming distinction that nonetheless conferred lasting prestige on both the individual athlete and his entire home city. Competitors who were discovered cheating, by stark contrast, were fined substantial sums, and this money financed the creation of bronze statues of Zeus engraved with the offenders' names, serving as a permanent public reminder of their dishonesty for generations afterward.

The ancient Games came to an end approximately 1,600 years ago, fading gradually as circumstances changed throughout the region. Centuries later, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin resolved to revive them, convinced that organized international athletic competition could cultivate healthy young people and promote genuinely peaceful relationships between nations. In 1896, the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens with athletes representing just 14 countries, and today competitors from more than 200 nations participate, with women now competing in nearly every sport on the modern program.

The Olympic flag displays five interlocking rings in blue, yellow, black, green, and red against a white background. Coubertin designed these rings specifically to symbolize the continents of the world united in friendship, and he observed with evident satisfaction that every national flag of his era contained at least one of these five particular colors somewhere within its design.

The Paralympic Games originated in a modest sports competition organized in England in 1948 by Dr. Ludwig Guttmann, a physician who incorporated structured athletic activity into the rehabilitation of soldiers suffering from spinal injuries. The first formal Paralympic Games took place in Rome in 1960, and today they are consistently held in the very same host city shortly after the conclusion of the Olympics, demonstrating persuasively that extraordinary athletic achievement takes many profoundly different forms.

Qualifying for either event demands years of sustained discipline, as athletes train almost daily, follow meticulously planned diets, prioritize physical recovery between sessions, and continually analyze their technique alongside experienced coaches and sports scientists.

Above all else, the Games celebrate fair play. Athletes consistently pledge to obey the established regulations and respect every opponent they face. Integrity ultimately matters considerably more than any single individual victory, a principle the ancient Greeks themselves had already recognized some three thousand years earlier.

versions.title: The Olympic Games: An Ancient Idea Reborn
versions.text:
Every four years, thousands of the world's most accomplished athletes assemble within a single host city to sprint, swim, leap, and throw before an enormous global television audience numbering in the billions. This international celebration is the Olympic Games, and its history stretches back nearly three thousand years to a tranquil valley situated in the western Peloponnese, a mountainous region of southern Greece that still draws visitors today.

The earliest Olympic Games took place in ancient Greece, and historians generally date the first formally recorded competition to 776 BCE, though the festival's actual origins likely predate even this. The festival itself was held at Olympia, a sacred sanctuary dedicated to Zeus, and it was so universally respected throughout the ancient Greek world that a formal truce allowed athletes and spectators alike to travel there in complete safety, even during periods when neighboring Greek city-states were actively engaged in military conflict with one another. Only men, however, were permitted to compete in these ancient contests, a restriction that stood for well over a thousand years. Initially, the entire program consisted of a single sprint measuring approximately 190 meters, but organizers progressively introduced wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, and various other physically demanding contests over the subsequent centuries that followed. Champions received no gold medals whatsoever; instead, each victor was crowned with a simple wreath of olive leaves, a modest-seeming distinction that nonetheless conferred lasting, far-reaching prestige on both the individual athlete and his entire home city for years afterward. Competitors who were discovered cheating, by stark and deliberate contrast, were fined substantial sums of money, and this money financed the creation of bronze statues of Zeus engraved permanently with the offenders' names, serving as a lasting public reminder of their dishonesty for generations of future visitors to see.

The ancient Games came to an end approximately 1,600 years ago, fading gradually as political and religious circumstances shifted throughout the broader region. Centuries later, a French educator named Pierre de Coubertin resolved deliberately to revive them, convinced firmly that organized international athletic competition could cultivate genuinely healthy young people and promote lasting, peaceful relationships between rival nations. In 1896, the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens with athletes representing just 14 countries in total, and today competitors from more than 200 nations participate on the same stage, with women now competing in nearly every single sport on the modern Olympic program, a profound transformation from the ancient original.

The Olympic flag displays five interlocking rings rendered in blue, yellow, black, green, and red against a plain white background. Coubertin designed these rings specifically to symbolize the continents of the world united peacefully in friendship, and he observed with evident personal satisfaction that every national flag of his own era contained at least one of these five particular colors somewhere within its overall design, a detail he considered meaningful.

The Paralympic Games originated in a comparatively modest sports competition organized in England in 1948 by Dr. Ludwig Guttmann, a physician who deliberately incorporated structured athletic activity into the rehabilitation of soldiers suffering from spinal injuries sustained during wartime. The first formal Paralympic Games subsequently took place in Rome in 1960, and today they are consistently held in the very same host city shortly after the conclusion of the Olympics themselves, demonstrating persuasively and repeatedly that extraordinary athletic achievement takes many profoundly different forms across different bodies and abilities.

Qualifying for either event demands years upon years of sustained personal discipline, as athletes train almost daily without exception, follow meticulously planned nutritional diets, deliberately prioritize physical recovery between demanding training sessions, and continually analyze their technique in close partnership with experienced coaches and dedicated sports scientists.

Above all else, the Games consistently celebrate the principle of fair play: athletes repeatedly pledge to obey the established regulations and respect every opponent they face on the field or track, because genuine integrity ultimately matters considerably more than any single individual victory ever could, a principle the ancient Greeks themselves had already recognized and formally enforced some three thousand years before the modern revival.

MID.prompt: Explain how the modern Olympic Games are similar to and different from the ancient Games. Use at least two details from the article to support your answer.
checklist: I gave at least one similarity and one difference.
I supported my answer with at least two details from the article.

MID.modelAnswer: The modern Olympic Games are both similar to and different from the ancient Games. Both events bring athletes together to compete and honor the idea of fair play, treating every opponent with respect. However, the ancient Games only allowed men to compete and gave winners a wreath of olive leaves, while the modern Games, which Pierre de Coubertin helped revive in 1896, now represent more than 200 nations, including both men and women. Another difference is that today the Paralympic Games represent athletes with a disability, something the ancient Games never had.

HIGH.prompt: Pierre de Coubertin believed that sport could encourage peace between nations. Do you agree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree with Pierre de Coubertin that sport can encourage peace between nations, because the modern Olympics were built on that very idea and the evidence supports it. The five interlocking rings symbolize continents joining together in friendship rather than conflict, and today athletes from more than two hundred countries compete side by side under shared rules of discipline and integrity. The Paralympic Games extend this spirit even further, since they celebrate rehabilitation and inclusion by giving athletes with disabilities the same stage as other competitors. Although the Olympics cannot end war on their own, much like the ancient Greek truce that paused conflict so athletes could travel safely to compete, the Games still demonstrate that nations can set aside rivalry for a shared celebration of fair competition.
